newsitem.title: USA: Gold hits three-year lows but bounces near close.
newsitem.headline: Gold hits three-year lows but bounces near close.

text.p: Gold prices fell to a three-year low Tuesday on renewed concerns about gold sales by European central banks and international mining houses, but managed to recover somewhat late in the day, traders said.
"The market remains confidently short, operating under protection of rumoured central bank and producer selling," said Chase Manhattan New York managing director Dinsa Mehta.

"We suspect there may have been a central bank sale in the past month and there has been some scattered selling by producers," he said. "The currency market is also a factor, with the U.S. dollar strong and volatility rising," he noted.

February gold ended down 50 cents at $370.40 an ounce on the New York Commodities Exchange after hitting a new life-of-contract low at $367.70 an ounce early in the day. Total estimated volume in gold futures was solid at 53,000 lots, traders said.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended at $368.40/368.90 an ounce, after gold was fixed in London Tuesday afternoon at $367.40 an ounce, its lowest level since November 1993.
Gold has been in a long-term downtrend from its five-year highs at $417.70 in February 1996.
Fears of European central bank sales, in preparation for the single European currency in 1999, have weighed on the market most of the year, analysts said.
On Nov. 24, even Switzerland, which has a quasi-gold standard, indicated it could consider selling gold.

The Swiss National Bank's chief legal counsel said the Federal Council of Switzerland was considering a proposal to remove the constitutional obligation to maintain gold stocks worth 40 percent of the Swiss currency in circulation and was looking at the possibility of selling part of its gold.
"We think this (Swiss) decision is a long-term bear point for gold because it means more and more central banks will consider mobilising their reserves," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said.
The strength of U.S. stock and bond markets has also removed the incentive for investors to buy gold, while currency movements have also been a factor, analysts said.

"Gold and silver demand from India has been slowing down sharply over the last six to eight weeks with the Bombay Bullion Market Association speaking of a 20 percent fall in gold demand during the recent Hindu Festival of Lights," Arnold said.

Strength in the Australian dollar and a partial recovery in the South African rand, which lowers the price of gold in those countries, has led to reports of hedging and forward sales by gold miners in those countries, analysts said.
In other trading, COMEX March silver ended up 10.3 cents at $4.845 an ounce after touching a new contract low at $4.710. Total estimated silver futures volume was 14,000 lots.

January platinum ended up 30 cents at $376.00 an ounce on the New York Mercantile Exchange after hitting a new contract low at $373.10, while March palladium closed down 60 cents at $117.25 an ounce after reaching a new contract low at $116.60.
